name: Acorn
description: Seven cells, 5,206 generations to settle. Small enough to type, large enough to fill a screen.
author: Charles Corderman

name: B-heptomino
description: The B-shaped seven. It throws off a block and keeps walking — grandparent of several puffers.
author: John H. Conway

name: Backward space rake
description: The same engine, firing over its shoulder. Gliders peel backward while the rake keeps going.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Bakery
description: Four loaves in a ring. The bakery produces nothing but the smell of still life.
author: unknown

name: Barge
description: A long diamond of six cells. The skinny cousin of the boat.
author: unknown

name: Beacon
description: Two blocks a knight-move apart. The inner corners flash on and off; the blocks never leave.
author: Simon Norton

name: Beacon pair 10
description: Two beacons offset by 10. Each blinks at the other from a polite distance.

description: A six-cell hexagon. Second-commonest still life in soup, after the block.

name: Bi-block
description: Two blocks a cell apart. The smallest interesting constellation: they do not touch, and they do not care.
author: unknown

name: Blinker
description: Three cells in a line that flip between horizontal and vertical every generation. Period 2, population 3.
author: John H. Conway

name: Blinker pair 10
description: Two blinkers 10 cells apart. They flip in sync and never touch.

name: Block agar
description: A finite patch of the block lattice. Every tile is a still life; together they are the dullest infinite wallpaper Life has.
author: unknown

name: Boat and ship
description: Two still lifes parked far enough apart that neither notices the other. Boat and ship.
author: unknown

name: Brian's Brain butterfly
description: A six-cell c/4 diagonal ship. Firing and cooling trade places every generation; the butterfly still walks.
author: fancy-gol

name: Brian's Brain p3
description: A period-3 oscillator in a rule with no period 2. Sweney found the first ones; this is the small square that blinks forever.
author: Michael Sweney

name: Brian's Brain photon
description: A lightspeed orthogonal photon. Eight cells of fire and ash covering four cells a generation.
author: fancy-gol

name: Brian's Brain seed 1
description: A firing-and-cooling spark unique to Brian's Brain. Phoenix rules: nothing survives, everything flashes.
author: fancy-gol

author: fancy-gol

name: Brian's Brain spark
description: Four firing cells around a cooling centre. In Brian's Brain they flash, decay, and scatter — a multi-state spark, not a Life still life.
author: Brian Silverman

name: Cis-mirrored R-bee
description: Two R-bees facing the same way. A honey-farm fragment that never left the hive.
author: unknown

name: Colour-changing reflector
description: A syringe welded to a Snark. Gliders leave on the other colour. The still-life waiting room of a 90-degree bounce.
author: unknown

name: Cross
description: A period-3 cross. The arms pull in and push out like a tiny plus sign doing yoga.
author: unknown

name: Day & Night seed
description: A compact Day & Night seed. Self-complementary rules treat this island differently than Conway ever would.
author: Nathan Thompson

name: Day & Night seed 1
description: A Day & Night island with a unique rim. Live and dead phases trade places more kindly than in Conway.

name: Dead spark coil
description: The spark coil after it stops sparking. Two hooks facing a gap that no longer fires.
author: unknown

name: Diagonal fuse
description: A staircase of dominoes. Light a corner and the wick burns at lightspeed along the diagonal.
author: unknown

name: Diamoeba blob 1
description: A diamond-ish Diamoeba seed. The rule pinches and sometimes throws wisps; this one is just the start.
author: fancy-gol

name: Diehard
description: Seven cells that live 130 generations and then leave nothing. A methuselah whose last trick is emptiness.
author: unknown

name: Eater 1
description: A seven-cell fishhook that can swallow gliders and still sit down afterwards. The original eater.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Figure eight
description: Two 3×3 blocks on a diagonal, trading mass for eight generations. Also called the big beacon.
author: unknown

name: Glider
description: Five cells that walk diagonally one cell every four generations. The smallest spaceship, and the one that made Life famous.
author: Richard K. Guy

name: Glider-producing switch engine
description: A switch engine that throws gliders as it crawls. A rake made of eight cells and patience.
author: Charles Corderman

name: Gosper glider gun
description: Two queen-bee shuttles back-to-back. Every 30 generations a glider leaves, and population never looks back.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Herschel
description: The heptomino that Life uses as a signal. Conduits, universal constructors and the Turing-complete circuitry of the late game all speak Herschel.
author: unknown

name: Highlands banding soup
description: The documented 32×32 banding soup from the Highlands / Liquid rule comments. Void, liquid and highland at 1/4, 3/8, 3/8 — the seed that settles into shorelines.
author: fancy-gol

name: Highlands puddle
description: A square of liquid. Weighted neighbours pull the shore inward until the puddle finds a quieter shape.
author: fancy-gol

name: Highlands ridge
description: A highland bar. Weight 3 on every neighbour makes a ridge that wants to stay land.
author: fancy-gol

name: Highlands shore
description: Land meeting water. The documented wall: highland on one side, liquid on the other, the threshold sitting on the beach.
author: fancy-gol

name: HighLife replicator
description: The reason HighLife has a fan club. A five-by-five that copies itself along the diagonal instead of sitting still.
author: unknown

name: HighLife seed
description: Eight cells that are not a Conway still life. HighLife's extra birth-on-6 is enough to pull this seed apart.
author: Nathan Thompson

name: HighLife seed 10
description: A compact HighLife seed with a unique barcode. Birth-on-6 pulls this one apart differently than Conway would.

name: Honey farm
description: Four beehives around an empty centre. A common ash of the traffic-light reaction.
author: unknown

name: Heavyweight spaceship
description: Thirteen cells, still c/2 orthogonal. The heaviest of the three standard spaceships Conway found in 1970.
author: John H. Conway

name: I-heptomino
description: Seven cells in a broken I. One of the heptominoes that runs a long time before sitting down.
author: unknown

name: Integral
description: Nine cells in an ∫-shape. A still life named for a joke about calculus, not for any calculus it performs.
author: unknown

name: Lidka
description: A small seed that takes thousands of generations to settle. Lidka is the patience test of the methuselah shelf.
author: Andrzej Okrasinski

name: Loaf
description: A seven-cell still life with a bite taken out of one corner. Stable, slightly lopsided.
author: unknown

name: Loaf and pond
description: Two still lifes parked far enough apart that neither notices the other. Loaf and pond.
author: unknown

name: Long barge
description: A barge with one extra pair of cells. Nine cells, still, and a step along the barge sequence.
author: unknown

name: Long boat
description: A boat stretched by one cell. Seven cells, still, and a step on the long-boat ladder.
author: unknown

name: Long canoe
description: A canoe stretched by one. Eight cells on a diagonal, still as a boat that forgot how to float.
author: unknown

name: Long ship
description: A ship with an extra row. Eight cells of still life, one longer than the namesake.
author: unknown

name: Life without Death flake 1
description: An inkspot flake. Cells never die, so this seed only stains more of the plane.
author: fancy-gol

name: Lightweight spaceship
description: Nine cells, period 4, c/2 along an axis. The smallest orthogonal spaceship.
author: John H. Conway

name: Mango
description: Eight cells with a diagonal shear. Sometimes called a cigar; it does not smoke.
author: unknown

name: Maze corridor 1
description: A corridor sketch for Maze. Survival on 1–5 freezes soup into walls; this seed is one brick.

name: Middleweight spaceship
description: The middle sibling of the XWSS family: eleven cells, same period and speed as the LWSS, one row taller.
author: John H. Conway

name: New gun 1
description: The second basic gun. Twin bees, a few eaters, and a glider every 46 generations.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Noah's ark
description: Two switch engines walking away from each other. An ark that unloads junk instead of animals.
author: unknown

name: Pentadecathlon
description: A row of ten, sparking at both ends on a 15-generation loop. Conway found it in the first month.
author: John H. Conway

name: Pi-heptomino
description: Seven cells in a pi shape. A short-lived methuselah and a common spark in larger machinery.
author: John H. Conway

name: Pond
description: An eight-cell ring around a 2×2 hole. Looks like a beehive that ate a block.
author: unknown

name: Pre-honey farm
description: The predecessor of the honey farm. Six cells that remember they wanted to be four beehives.
author: unknown

name: Puffer 2
description: Two lightweight ships escort a B-heptomino. The second puffer anyone found, and it still drops junk every 140 generations.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Pulsar
description: Forty-eight cells in four-fold symmetry, breathing on a 13×13 stage every three generations.
author: John H. Conway

name: Queen bee shuttle
description: A queen-bee spark bounces between two blocks every 30 generations. The oscillator that taught guns to exist.
author: Bill Gosper

name: R-pentomino
description: Five cells that refuse to sit down for 1,103 generations. The methuselah that started the hunt.
author: John H. Conway

name: Rabbits
description: Nine cells that multiply like the name before the ash wins. A compact methuselah from Trevorrow.
author: Andrew Trevorrow

name: Replicator seed 1
description: A Fredkin-rule seed. Odd neighbourhoods copy; this barcode is the serial number on the tile.

description: Puffer 2 plus two lightweight ships — the recipe Riley used for a tiny quadratic-growth breeder.
author: Mitchell Riley

name: Schick engine
description: Two lightweight ships towing a period-12 spark. The tagalong that taught puffers to have engines.
author: Paul Schick

name: Seeds cluster
description: Twelve cells packed into a 4×4. In Seeds every live cell dies, so this is a fuse, not a still life.

description: A Seeds fuse with a unique barcode. Every live cell dies; the next generation is born from pairs.

description: A Spartan 90-degree reflector that keeps every other glider. The still-life bait, waiting for a stream.
author: unknown

name: Ship
description: A six-cell still life, boat plus one. Not a spaceship — it sits there.
author: unknown

name: Ship and pond
description: Two still lifes parked far enough apart that neither notices the other. Ship and pond.
author: unknown

name: Ship tie
description: Two ships sharing a side. Twelve cells, one object — a still-life siamese, not a collision in progress.
author: unknown

name: Snake
description: Six cells in a 4×2 S-bend. Flat, snappy, and easy to miss in a stamp sheet.
author: unknown

name: Space rake
description: A moving factory: the rake crawls at c/2 and throws a glider forward every twenty generations.
author: Bill Gosper

name: Stairstep hexomino
description: Six cells on a stair. It settles into the blockade — four blocks in a diamond — and then stops climbing.
author: unknown

name: Star Wars seed 1
description: A Star Wars filament seed. Born on 3–5, it ages through two decaying states and looks like a dogfight.

name: Switch engine
description: The original messy puffer: a eight-cell engine that crawls and leaves junk. Stabilised cousins become clean puffers and rakes.
author: Charles Corderman

name: T-tetromino
description: Four cells in a T. The smallest interesting seed: it becomes a traffic light and then sits down.
author: unknown

name: Thunderbird
description: A T of six cells. It runs for a couple of hundred generations, then the usual junk.
author: unknown

name: Toad
description: Two offset rows of three. They rock past each other every generation — a p2 neighbour of the blinker.

name: WireWorld AND
description: A pocket that wants two heads at once. One input alone dies in the gap; both together spawn an output electron.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld clock
description: A four-cell loop with one electron. The clock ticks forever and feeds every gate that needs a heartbeat.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld crossover
description: A plus-shaped crossing. Electrons that arrive on one axis leave on the same axis if the timing is kind.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld delay
description: A long rail. Same electron, more generations — the delay line every adder eventually asks for.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld diode
description: A one-way conductor gap. Electrons that approach from the tail side pass; the other direction dies in the pocket.
author: Brian Silverman

name: WireWorld fan-out
description: A T-junction. One electron becomes two, which is how clocks feed more than one gate.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld half adder
description: A compact half-adder sketch: XOR-ish sum and AND-ish carry sharing a box of conductor. A starting kit, not a silicon die.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld OR
description: Two rails join a trunk. One or two incoming heads both fire the output — WireWorld’s native OR.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld terminator
description: A rail that simply ends. Electrons arrive, find nowhere to go, and vanish. The period at the end of a sentence.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld wire
description: A straight conductor with one electron already on the rail. The simplest moving signal in the rule.
author: fancy-gol

name: WireWorld XOR
description: Two inputs, one output, and a crossing that cancels doubles. Exclusive-or drawn in conductor.
